title: How to stream live sports without cable: 5 options

 Five ways to stream live sports without cable, from live TV bundles to league apps and free over-the-air antennas, and what each option covers
 1 / 7 List slides 5 ways to stream live sports without cable List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated October 30, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 Live sports were, for years, the main reason many households kept a cable subscription. Movies and scripted series moved to on-demand streaming, but a game matters most while it is happening. The channels that carried most of those games sat inside cable packages.
 That link has loosened. Leagues now sell their own subscriptions. Broadcast networks run streaming services that carry some games. Internet-delivered channel bundles replicate much of a cable lineup without a set-top box. The oldest method of all, a broadcast antenna, still picks up local stations with no monthly fee.
 The result is more choice, along with more fragmentation. Anyone who wants to stream live sports without cable is no longer buying a single package. They are assembling one from services, apps and hardware, each covering a different slice of the sports calendar. One option may carry national broadcasts but not a regional sports network. Another may show a full league schedule while restricting some games in a viewer's home market. A free option may offer plenty of programming but little of the live, major-league action a fan is looking for.
 Working out the right mix starts with three questions. Which leagues and teams matter most? Are the important games local, national or out of market? Which devices will be used to watch them? The answers can point to a combination of two or three tools rather than one.
 The five approaches below are a selection of ways to watch sports without cable. They include live TV streaming services and subscription apps sold by leagues and sports networks. A digital antenna covers over-the-air broadcasts. The list also covers entertainment streamers that carry selected live events, along with free ad-supported streaming channels. Each one works differently, bills differently and covers a different set of games.
 Sports rights change often. Leagues sign new deals, games move between networks and services add or drop channels from one season to the next. Before paying for any of them, confirm the current lineup and game coverage directly with each provider.
 Live TV streaming services like YouTube TV and Fubo 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Live TV streaming services such as YouTube TV, Sling TV, Fubo and Hulu + Live TV deliver packages of cable-style channels over the internet. For sports fans, they are the closest substitute for a traditional cable lineup. National sports networks and, in many markets, local broadcast stations sit together in one app.
 The industry term for this category is virtual multichannel video programming distributor, often shortened to vMVPD. These services carry the same live linear channels a cable or satellite operator would, on the same schedule. A game airs live on whichever channel holds it, just as it would on cable.
 Billing runs month to month. Subscribers can generally cancel without an early termination fee, unlike many cable and satellite contracts. That structure lets a viewer sign up for one sport's season and drop the service when the season ends.
 Most of these services include a cloud DVR. Recordings are stored on the provider's servers rather than on a box in the living room. Storage limits and the length of time recordings are kept differ by provider and plan.
 Local channels are the main variable. Whether a service carries a particular market's CBS, NBC, Fox or ABC affiliate depends on agreements with the companies that own those stations. Coverage can differ from one city to the next. The services also use a subscriber's location to decide which local stations and games appear. A home area set at signup can affect what is available while traveling.
 Regional sports networks are another point to check. These channels carry many local professional games. Their availability across live TV streaming services is uneven, and it shifts as carriage deals are renewed or dropped.
 Each service caps how many streams can play at the same time on one account. Households where several people watch different games should look at that limit before choosing.
 The apps run on major smart TV platforms, streaming players such as Roku $ROKU , Apple $AAPL TV and Amazon $AMZN Fire TV, phones, tablets and web browsers. Support for individual devices varies by service. A steady broadband connection is required. High-resolution live sports use more bandwidth than standard-definition video.
 Comparing each service's channel list against the specific national and regional networks that carry a viewer's teams shows which one covers them.
 League apps like NFL+, NBA League Pass and MLB.TV 
 Illustration: Quartz
 League-run streaming apps such as NFL+, NBA League Pass and MLB.TV sell coverage of a single sport directly to fans, with no cable subscription required. NBA League Pass and MLB.TV in particular suit viewers who follow a team based outside their local market.
 Each app comes from the league itself. NFL+ is the National Football League's own subscription service. NBA League Pass is the National Basketball Association's package of games. MLB.TV is Major League Baseball's streaming product. Because the league runs each service, the focus is narrow and deep: one sport, many games and little other programming.
 The core use case is distance. A Boston Red Sox fan living in Seattle generally cannot watch the team's regular broadcasts on local Seattle television. Out-of-market packages exist to close that gap. They give relocated fans a way to follow a team across a full season from another city or region.
 NFL+ is built differently. It is not the NFL's out-of-market package. The live games and devices it covers are set by the league's current terms. Football fans following a distant team should check which NFL product carries those games.
 The trade-off sits in the home market. Local TV rights for many teams belong to regional broadcasters. League apps are often restricted from showing those games inside a team's own territory. A fan who lives near their team may find that a league app does not carry the games they most want to see.
 Nationally televised games can fall under separate terms as well. The rules differ by league and can change from season to season. The league's own terms are the place to confirm exactly which games a subscription includes.
 Beyond live games, these apps commonly add on-demand features. Full-game replays let viewers watch after a game ends. Condensed games cut a full contest down to its key plays for faster catch-up.
 ESPN's direct-to-consumer streaming service fills a related role from a different angle. Instead of covering one league, it is organized around a network and carries events from several sports. Its event lineup depends on ESPN's rights agreements. Those are worth checking before subscribing.
 Households that follow more than one sport can combine league apps. Basketball and baseball seasons only partly overlap, so a fan of both might hold each app during its own season. Availability and terms also vary by country. Viewers outside the U.S. should check the version of each app offered where they live.
 Digital antenna for free over-the-air sports broadcasts 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A digital antenna lets a TV pick up local broadcast stations for free, with no subscription and no internet connection. Local affiliates of major networks such as CBS, NBC, Fox and ABC air many high-profile sporting events. For those games, an antenna is a low-cost way to watch live.
 Over-the-air broadcasting works differently from streaming. Local stations transmit their signals from towers. Any TV with a built-in digital tuner can decode those signals once an antenna is connected. Older sets without one need a separate converter box or tuner.
 The current system dates to June 12, 2009, when full-power U.S. stations completed the switch from analog to digital broadcasting. Digital reception behaves differently from the old analog signal. A weak analog channel faded into a snowy picture. A weak digital channel tends to freeze, break into blocks or drop out entirely.
 Reception depends on location. Distance from broadcast towers, terrain, tall buildings and the materials in a home's walls all affect which stations come in. The FCC offers a DTV reception maps tool that estimates which channels should be available at a given address. It also shows how strong each signal is likely to be. Checking it before buying hardware helps a viewer decide between an indoor and an outdoor model.
 Indoor antennas are small, flat or compact units placed near a window or high on a wall. They suit viewers who live close to transmitters. Outdoor and attic-mounted antennas sit higher and face fewer obstructions. That placement generally helps them pull in more distant stations.
 Some models include an amplifier, which can offset signal loss on long cable runs. An amplifier cannot create a signal that is not reaching the antenna in the first place. Labels such as "HD antenna" are marketing terms. Any antenna built for the VHF and UHF bands can receive digital broadcasts.
 An antenna can also feed other hardware. An over-the-air DVR records games for later viewing. A networked tuner can send antenna channels to phones, tablets and streaming devices around the home.
 The newer U.S. broadcast standard, ATSC 3.0, is marketed as NextGen TV. Watching those broadcasts requires a compatible TV or tuner. Availability depends on whether local stations in a given market have adopted the standard. Existing antennas generally work with it.
 An antenna covers only what local stations air. Games carried exclusively on cable networks or streaming services will not appear over the air. Viewers should check local listings for the specific events they follow.
 Peacock, Paramount+ and other streamers with live sports 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Peacock and Paramount $PARA + are general entertainment streaming services that also carry selected live sports. Each is owned by a media company with a broadcast network, which gives it access to some of the same events that air on traditional TV.
 Peacock belongs to NBCUniversal, the Comcast $CMCSA -owned company behind the NBC broadcast network. It launched nationally in July 2020. Paramount + belongs to Paramount , the parent of CBS. The service took its current name in March 2021, replacing CBS All Access.
 That corporate link shapes what each service offers. Some live events stream on the app at the same time they air on the parent company's broadcast network. Others stream only on the app, with no over-the-air or cable broadcast at all. A fan who relies on a single viewing method can miss games distributed that way.
 The sports sit inside a much larger catalog of movies, series and news. Coverage is selective rather than comprehensive. A subscription may include some games from a league or a few major events without covering every game of a full season.
 Each service sells more than one plan, and the plans do not always include the same live content. Some live programming, including a local broadcast station feed, may be limited to a particular tier. The plan details on each provider's own site are the place to confirm what a given subscription includes.
 These services can work as seasonal purchases. A viewer can subscribe for the stretch of a season or a single event, then cancel once it ends. The approach fits fans who follow a few specific competitions rather than an entire league.
 Other general streamers beyond Peacock and Paramount + have also added live sports alongside their on-demand libraries. Their event lineups can shift from year to year. The current schedule on each service is worth checking before signing up.
 Free ad-supported streaming TV channels for sports 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Free ad-supported streaming TV, known as FAST, offers sports channels at no cost through platforms such as Pluto TV, Tubi and The Roku $ROKU Channel. Viewers watch advertising instead of paying a subscription fee. The sports on offer lean toward highlights and replays rather than major-league live games.
 FAST services are built to feel like traditional television. They do more than offer a library of titles to pick from. They also run scheduled channels with a program guide, and a viewer flips between them the way they once flipped through cable. Commercial breaks interrupt the programming at regular intervals. No credit card or payment details are needed to start watching.
 Each of these three services sits inside a larger media or technology company. Pluto TV belongs to Paramount $PARA . Tubi is owned by Fox Corporation. The Roku Channel is run by Roku , the streaming device maker, though its app is not limited to Roku hardware. TV manufacturers have entered the space too. Samsung TV Plus comes built into Samsung smart TVs.
 Sports programming on these platforms tends to fall into a few categories. There are highlight reels, studio talk and analysis shows, classic games from past seasons and sports documentaries. Some leagues and sports media companies run their own branded channels, filled largely with archival footage and recaps. Live coverage does appear. It usually involves niche sports, lower-tier competitions or events outside the major U.S. leagues.
 That mix makes FAST a supplement to a sports setup, not a replacement for one. A fan who wants every regular-season game of a major team will still need another service. A fan who wants background sports coverage, replays of past games or exposure to less familiar sports can find it here without paying.
 Channel lineups on FAST services change often, and they differ from country to country. Pluto TV operates in the U.K. and several other markets outside the U.S. Its channel lineup in those countries is not the same as the American version. A platform's current guide shows which sports channels it carries at any given time.
